rows: Identify the common base 2; the two powers have exponents 2 and 3.
scenes.misconception: Same base: add exponents, never bases.

rows: Identify the same nonzero base 3 in numerator and denominator.
Expand the numerator into 4 factors of 3.
Expand the denominator into 2 factors of 3.
Cancel 2 matching nonzero factor pairs; 2 factors remain.
scenes.memo: 81 ÷ 9 = 9; division of the original powers agrees.
scenes.misconception: Cancel equal nonzero factor pairs before subtracting exponents.

scenes.problem: Use an exponent law to evaluate 8⁰.
rows: Write 8² ÷ 8²; equal nonzero quantities divide to 1.
Apply the quotient law to the same expression: 8^(2−2) = 8⁰.
Do not mistake the zero exponent for multiplication by zero.
scenes.misconception: A nonzero base to exponent zero equals one.

rows: Identify the common base 5; the two powers have exponents 3 and 2.

scenes.problem: Use a power-of-a-product law to evaluate 6² by factoring 6 as 2 × 3.
rows: Expand into 2 copies of (2 × 3); this is multiplication, not addition.
scenes.memo: 6² = 36; raising the original whole base gives the same result.
scenes.misconception: Only products allow this law: (3+2)² = 25, whereas 3²+2² = 13. Factor the original base as a multiplication first.

scenes.problem: Simplify and evaluate 3⁴ × 3² ÷ 3³. Show each exponent law.
rows: All three powers share nonzero base 3; the exponents are 4, 2 and 3.
Divide by 3³; cancel 3 matching factors from numerator and denominator.
scenes.misconception: Combine equal bases in the numerator, then cancel nonzero factors before subtracting exponents.
